concept.technique_name: sector area as a fraction of the full circle

examples.problem_statement: The minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. Find the area of the face of the clock described by the minute hand between 9 a.m. and 9 : 35 a.m.

solution.description: Start from the fact the book's solution opens with: one complete sweep of the minute hand covers the whole dial, which is 360 degrees.
Convert the 35 minutes of travel into the angle the hand traverses on that dial; the book records this sweep as 210 degrees.
Take the swept angle as a fraction of the full turn and apply that fraction to the area of the circle of radius 10 cm (the hand length), giving the area described.

key_reminders: The full clock dial is 360 degrees, and the minute hand sweeps all of it in 60 minutes.
A sector's area is the fraction (angle / 360) of the whole circle's area \pi r^2.
The radius of the swept sector is the length of the minute hand, 10 cm.
common_mistakes: Using 35 directly as the angle instead of converting 35 minutes into the 210 degrees the hand traverses.
Computing arc length (a fraction of 2 \pi r) instead of sector area (a fraction of \pi r^2).

concept.technique_name: multiplication by 12 (double each digit and add its neighbour)

examples.problem_statement: Multiplication by 12 — rule: double each digit in turn and add its neighbour (the digit to its right). Solve: 5324 x 12

solution.description: Write a leading zero in front of the number so the left-most digit also has a digit to double when the sweep reaches it.
Start at the right-most digit, 4: double it. There is no neighbour to its right, so 8 is written as the units digit of the answer.
Move left to 2: double it and add its right neighbour 4, giving 8, which is placed in the tens position.
Move left to 3: double it and add its right neighbour 2, giving 8, placed in the hundreds position.
Move left to 5: double it and add its right neighbour 3, giving 13; write the 3 and carry the 1 into the next position.
Finish on the leading zero: double it, add its right neighbour 5 and the carried 1, giving 6 as the left-most digit of the product.

key_reminders: Each output digit is (2 x current digit) + (digit immediately to its right).
Prefix a zero so the left-most real digit is processed like every other digit.
Any two-digit intermediate result leaves its units digit in place and carries the tens digit leftwards.
common_mistakes: Dropping the leading-zero step and stopping at 3888, losing the leading 6.
Forgetting to add the carry of 1 from the 2 x 5 + 3 = 13 step into the final position.

examples.problem_statement: Either Raghav is sick or he is stoned. (i) Raghav is sick. (ii) Raghav is not sick. (iii) Raghav is stoned. (iv) Raghav is not stoned. Which pair is such that the second statement follows logically from the first?

solution.result: at least one of the two holds
solution.description: Take the given statement at face value: it asserts that Raghav is sick or he is stoned, so the two possibilities cannot both fail.
Eliminate one branch: if he is not stoned, the remaining option must hold, so he must be sick — that is, statement (i) follows from statement (iv).
Match that ordered pair, (iv) leading to (i), against the answer choices and pick the option listing iv-i.

key_reminders: An inclusive 'either A or B' guarantees that denying one alternative forces the other.
The listed pair is ordered: the second statement must follow from the first.
common_mistakes: Choosing i-iii, treating the two alternatives as implying each other rather than as alternatives.
Getting the pair's direction backwards and picking a pair that reads (i) then (iv).
